title: Approach to Syncope: Bedside Diagnosis and Risk Stratification
summary: Syncope evaluation begins with targeted history, physical exam, and a 12‑lead ECG—these alone establish a cause in many patients and determine short‑term risk. Use validated tools cautiously; clinician gestalt plus red flags outperform any single score. Admit or closely monitor patients with high‑risk features; otherwise, discharge with prompt follow‑up and selective testing.
clinicalQuestion: In adults presenting with syncope, how should clinicians perform bedside diagnosis and short-term risk stratification to guide testing, disposition, and follow-up?

heroStats.label: ECG diagnostic yield
heroStats.value: Identifies cardiac cause or high risk in ≈5–10% [1], [3]

keyMoments.title: Start with bedside triad
keyMoments.body: Focused history, orthostatic vitals, and a 12‑lead ECG diagnose or risk‑stratify most patients; abnormal ECG or exertional syncope are pivotal cardiac clues [1], [3].

keyMoments.title: Identify high‑risk features
keyMoments.body: Consider admission/telemetry for structural heart disease, syncope during exertion or supine, abnormal ECG, hypotension, anemia/bleeding, or troponin elevation [1], [2], [4].

keyMoments.title: Use scores to calibrate risk
keyMoments.body: CSRS and FAINT can complement—but not replace—clinical judgment for 30‑day serious outcomes, especially in older adults [2], [4], [5].

keyMoments.title: Test selectively
keyMoments.body: Avoid routine CT, EEG, or extensive labs; target echocardiography, ambulatory monitoring, or tilt based on history and ECG [1], [3], [6].

sections.title: Rapid, Structured Evaluation in the ED/Clinic
sections.blurb: A focused approach clarifies etiology and immediate risk while minimizing low‑value testing.

steps.title: Confirm true syncope and immediate safety
steps.body: Differentiate syncope (transient global cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid recovery) from seizure, TIA, falls, or psychogenic pseudosyncope. Assess airway, breathing, circulation; obtain pulse oximetry and finger‑stick glucose if altered. Look for trauma from the fall and active bleeding [1], [3].

steps.title: Focused history: the 6 anchors
steps.body: 1) Context: exertional or supine events suggest cardiac causes; prolonged standing or heat favors reflex syncope. 2) Prodrome: nausea, warmth, or diaphoresis points to vasovagal; none suggests arrhythmic. 3) Triggers: micturition, defecation, cough, or pain imply situational reflex. 4) Cardiac history: heart failure, prior MI, cardiomyopathy are high risk. 5) Medications: antihypertensives, diuretics, QT‑prolonging drugs. 6) Injury pattern: severe trauma without prodrome suggests arrhythmia [1], [3].

steps.title: Examination and orthostatics
steps.body: Measure supine and standing blood pressure and heart rate; **orthostatic hypotension** supports volume depletion or autonomic failure. Auscultate for murmurs (aortic stenosis, HCM), assess carotid bruits when appropriate, and perform a brief neuro exam; focal deficits argue against syncope as primary diagnosis [1], [3].

steps.title: 12‑lead ECG and targeted labs
steps.body: Identify conduction disease, ischemia, pre‑excitation, Brugada pattern, QT prolongation, or ventricular hypertrophy. Obtain troponin if ischemia suspected; pregnancy test in women of childbearing potential; hemoglobin if bleeding suspected. Routine broad panels have low yield without clinical indication [1], [3].

steps.title: Classify likely mechanism
steps.body: Vasovagal/situational (common, benign), orthostatic hypotension, cardiac arrhythmia, or structural cardiac syncope. When the mechanism is unclear but risk is low, outpatient monitoring clarifies diagnosis while avoiding unnecessary admission [1], [2], [6].

sections.title: Who Requires Monitoring or Admission?
sections.blurb: Combine red flags with validated tools to estimate 30‑day serious adverse events (SAE).

cards.title: High‑risk features (admit/telemetry)
items: Syncope during exertion or while supine; palpitations at onset [1], [3]
Abnormal ECG: ischemia, high‑grade AV block, wide QRS, long QT, Brugada, WPW [1], [3]
Structural heart disease or heart failure; reduced LVEF; prior MI [1], [2]
Systolic BP <90 mmHg, persistent tachy/bradyarrhythmia, or trauma from syncope [1], [2]
Active bleeding, Hgb markedly low, or rising troponin without alternative explanation [1], [2]

cards.title: Low‑risk features (safe discharge with follow‑up)
items: Typical vasovagal prodrome; event with prolonged standing or heat [1], [3]
Normal vitals after observation; normal ECG [1], [3]
No known structural heart disease; no concerning comorbidities [1], [2]
CSRS low/very low risk: **30‑day SAE ≈0.3–0.7%** [2], [4]

cards.title: Use of risk scores
items: Canadian Syncope Risk Score (CSRS): integrates history, ECG, troponin, and ED diagnosis; strong discrimination in derivation and external validation (**AUROC ≈0.88–0.91**) [2], [4]
FAINT score for adults ≥60 y: helps exclude 30‑day SAE; low‑risk threshold yields **sensitivity ~96–97%** with **NPV >98%** [5]
San Francisco Syncope Rule: early tool with variable external performance; not recommended as sole arbiter [1]

cards.title: Targeted diagnostics after ED
items: Echocardiography: if murmur, known heart disease, or abnormal ECG [1], [3]
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring: Holter or patch (frequent events); external loop/ILR for infrequent unexplained syncope—ILR increases diagnostic yield and time‑to‑diagnosis benefit [1], [6]
Tilt‑table testing: recurrent suspected reflex syncope or delayed orthostatic intolerance when bedside orthostatics are non‑diagnostic [1]
Carotid sinus massage in patients >40 y with compatible history and no carotid bruit [1]

cards.title: Observation and follow‑up
items: Short ED observation with serial ECG/troponin when ischemia or arrhythmia suspected but unclear [2]
Discharge low‑risk patients with return precautions and follow‑up in 48–72 h if symptoms recur or if outpatient monitoring arranged [2], [4]

cards.title: Management pearls
items: Vasovagal: education, hydration, counter‑pressure maneuvers; consider fludrocortisone or midodrine selectively [1]
Orthostatic: review medications (diuretics, alpha‑blockers), volume repletion, compression, gradual position changes [1]
Arrhythmic/structural: guideline‑directed therapy; pacemaker/ICD evaluation when indicated [1], [3]
